papers.title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
papers.abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.

papers.title: Optimal Operating-Point Selection for Single-Linearization Trajectory Planning of Nonlinear Robot Manipulators
papers.abstract: Single-point linearization provides a computationally efficient basis for optimization-based trajectory planning of nonlinear robot manipulators. However, planning performance depends on the selected linearization point. This paper presents an offline performance-driven approach that treats the location of a single linearization as an optimization variable. Candidate operating points are sampled from a common cubic seed trajectory, and each corresponding affine model is used to solve an identical constrained finite-horizon quadratic program (QP). The resulting control sequences are executed on the original nonlinear dynamics, and the operating point minimizing the nonlinear trajectory objective is selected through grid search and bounded refinement. Evaluation on four point-to-point motions of a three-degree-of-freedom UR5 manipulator yields optimal normalized operating-point locations between 0.325 and 0.935, demonstrating trajectory-dependent selection. Compared with the best-performing conventional initial, midpoint, or terminal linearization, the proposed approach reduces the nonlinear trajectory objective by 17-18%, 21-22%, 37-38%, and 7-8% across the four tasks, respectively. Additional nonlinear execution with identical PID feedback correction confirms that the performance advantage persists for a representative task. These results demonstrate that systematic operating-point selection can substantially improve single-linearization trajectory planning while preserving a fixed affine planning model.

papers.title: Correcting Persistent Failures in Point-Cloud Grasping Policies using Human Demonstrations in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.

papers.title: Passage-Focused Soft Coordination for Hierarchical Multi-Robot Navigation in Bottleneck Environments
papers.abstract: In multi-robot navigation, rigid global schedules are sensitive to execution deviations, while local methods lack long-horizon coordination. We propose a passage-focused framework combining soft global coordination with flexible local execution. A passage-induced graph of convex sets supports priority-ordered planning with two levels of soft coordination. Passage-aware route selection accounts for passage usage and traversal directions, while route-restricted continuous space-time planning penalizes temporal conflicts. The resulting references guide a model predictive path integral controller that avoids collisions online. Adaptive temporal and geometric tracking accommodates execution deviations, while selective replanning maintains coordination without rigid trajectory reservations. Across 1,200 instances in 4 different environments with 5-30 robots, the framework achieves a near-perfect success rate and outperforms evaluated baselines in makespan and flowtime. Hardware experiments with 8 robots demonstrate successful completion of all trials without collisions. These results highlight the effectiveness of passage-focused coordination in balancing long-horizon cooperation with flexible execution.

papers.title: Technical Report of Auriga's 1:10 Scale Autonomous Vehicle Robot
papers.abstract: This report presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle, developed at Shahid Beheshti University's Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory. The platform integrates a custom mechanical chassis, a distributed embedded system based on ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX module for high-level perception and control. The embedded layer manages sensor interfacing, real-time data acquisition, and actuator control, while the Jetson handles environment perception through deep-learning--based lane, sign, and traffic light detection, as well as decision-making and trajectory control. System communication is achieved via structured UART links, ensuring synchronized operation between perception and control subsystems. The vehicle's software stack incorporates ROS, modular firmware design, and multiple control algorithms---Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit---to achieve stable autonomous navigation in structured driving scenarios. The overall system demonstrates robust performance and reliability in urban-like environments, serving as a modular research platform for future autonomous driving studies.

papers.title: Robustness as a Transferable Skill: Cross-Task Adversarial Defense for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

papers.title: Data-Driven Predictive Control for Autonomous Vehicle Racing under Varying Friction
papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DPC) predicts future outputs by combining recorded input-output trajectory data such that the combined trajectory approximately matches a measured initial trajectory and tracks a provided reference. This paper investigates to what extent and under which conditions DPC using data pooled across operating conditions retains the prediction accuracy of DPC using data from the current operating condition. In autonomous vehicle racing, the tire-road friction varies between racetrack sections and tire sets. If the initial trajectory and the recorded data originate from different frictions, prediction accuracy of DPC degrades. Ensuring the frictions match requires knowing the friction during recording and estimating the current friction explicitly. Instead, we pool data recorded at different frictions. We compare the prediction accuracy of DPC using data recorded under the current friction (matched), a different friction (mismatched) and data pooled from both frictions. We evaluate in simulation and small-scale vehicle experiments in the Cyber-Physical Mobility Lab (CPM Lab). Our results show that pooled data keep the multi-step root-mean-square prediction error within 1.5 times that of matched data, whereas mismatched data increase it by a factor of 2.2 to 3.4. To assess how this prediction accuracy carries over to control, we evaluate the tracking error from the raceline in closed loop. In simulation, DPC with pooled data tracks comparably to nonlinear model predictive control (13.7 cm versus 13.3 cm) and close to DPC with matched data in the CPM Lab, differing by 0.1 cm on the low-friction tires (1.6 cm versus 1.5 cm) and by 0.2 cm on the high-friction tires (0.9 cm versus 1.1 cm). DPC thus provides partial adaptation to varying friction, without a dedicated adaptation method.

papers.title: Déjà-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating
papers.abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present Déjà-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from Déjà View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

papers.title: MVSTF: Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion for LiDAR-Based Moving Object Segmentation
papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots confront significant chal lenges in recognizing the motion properties of objects in dy namic environments. However, existing methods are hindered by limitations such as boundary ambiguity, occlusion, viewpoint constraints, and training complexity. In this paper, we propose an innovative end-to-end Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion network, named MVSTF, which utilizes sequential point clouds to generate multi-view images and feature differences, and designs a multi-branch network to extract spatio-temporal and dimen sional features in parallel, and realizes high-precision moving object segmentation. First, sequential point clouds are utilized to generate multi-view images and feature differences. Then, an end-to-end multi-branch network including Dual Down-sampling Blocks (DDB), Spatial Attention Blocks (SAB), Multi-Kernel Convolutional Neural Network blocks (MKCNN), Dual Feature Fusion Blocks (DFFB), and the Point Fusion (PF) module, is designed to extract motion features from feature differences and geometric and semantic features from multi-view images. Finally, an auxiliary semantic head is introduced to further improve the algorithm's robustness and the model's interpretability. This work is validated on the SemanticKITTI and KITTI-Road bench marks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the SemanticKITTI MOS validation set and the KITTI-Road validation set, and competitive results on the hidden SemanticKITTI-MOS test set. The code is available at this https URL .

papers.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
papers.abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

papers.title: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation
papers.abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

papers.title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

papers.title: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data
papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.

papers.title: VoxSAOR: Semantic-Aware Occupancy Robustification via Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling
papers.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at this https URL .

papers.title: Course-Referenced Lateral Control of Trail-Following Convoys: String Stability and Adaptive Feedforward under Load Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Vehicles in a convoy can steer along the GNSS trails of the vehicles ahead when lane markings are unavailable, as on snow covered roads. Since each vehicle's tracking error enters the reference of the next, lateral errors can grow along the convoy. This paper presents a course referenced formulation of trail following in arc length, in which each follower takes the direction of its fitted trail as its heading reference. Error propagation then reduces to a single transfer function. We derive a condition under which combining the trails of the leader and the predecessor keeps the errors bounded for any convoy length, and show that following the predecessor alone lets the errors accumulate without bound, even without amplification, on roads that end turned or shifted sideways. Passenger and cargo loads and tire stiffness vary in practice, and we show that they enter the curvature feedforward through a single coefficient, whose mismatch leaves steady offsets on curves. We propose an adaptive law that estimates this coefficient on curves and removes the offsets. Simulations of an eleven vehicle convoy confirm the analysis.

papers.title: Aerial Person Detection under Edge Constraints: Held-Out Evaluation and Edge-Ground Verification
papers.abstract: A search drone sees a missing person as a few pixels, carries a small computer, and shares a narrow radio link. We study person detection under those limits; the primary evaluations were declared before they ran, and later analyses are marked exploratory. In an exploratory comparison, holding out recording blocks inferred from thermal frame identifiers cut recall at a fixed false-alarm target from 32.7% to 12.3%. With nothing tuned on test blocks, a 46,000-parameter detector gated by a contrast cue finds 10.4% of people against 5.7% for the same network applied everywhere. A standard detector, YOLO11n, trained under the same folds finds 54.5% at a similar false-alarm rate for about eleven times the arithmetic, and on our 4K field footage at 117 m has a walking person among its top 16 detections in up to 92% of frames against 74% for our board. Run alone, YOLO11n's thresholds set at one location overshot their false-alarm target 1.7 to 3.4 times at new locations, and its best configuration at altitude cost 4 to 24 standard passes per frame. Re-scoring its 16 best crops (154 KB per frame) with an 842,000-parameter ground model, thresholds frozen on a validation location, raised recall from 44.9% to 53.7% against the same 16 crops with YOLO's own scores; in a post hoc paired analysis over 15 test locations the gain was +8.8 points [+2.4, +12.5]. Pooled false detections fell from 0.86 to 0.64 per frame, but that paired change was not distinguishable from zero. Coverage of a still person in earth tones was very low for both detectors in the clips we flew.

papers.title: A Geometric Observer for Visual-Inertial Odometry using Optical-Flow Constraints
papers.abstract: This paper presents a geometric observer for monocular visual-inertial odometry driven by individual optical-flow constraints. For each tracked point, the bearing and its rotationally compensated derivative give a depth-free homogeneous constraint on the body-frame velocity. These constraints enter the innovation of an observer on the gravity-augmented group $\mathbb{SE}_3(3)$ through a Riccati gain, without estimating depths or reconstructing the direction of motion. The auxiliary gravity state makes the six-dimensional body-frame velocity-gravity error dynamics independent of the attitude correction, and their uniform observability is shown to be equivalent to persistent excitation of a matrix formed from the inertial bearings and their derivatives. Under this condition, the body-frame velocity and gravity errors converge globally and uniformly exponentially, and a gravity-based attitude correction renders the combined velocity, gravity, and reduced-attitude error almost globally asymptotically stable and locally uniformly exponentially stable. Simulations illustrate the excitation condition, recovery from initial errors, and sensitivity to perturbed measurements.

papers.title: D'BEAST: Logged Bad Experiences as Explanation for Autonomous Driving Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents learn from mistakes, yet their decisions can be difficult to trace back to those experiences. We investigate whether a tabular agent's decisions can be explained by its bad experiences, defined as the training transitions associated with safety or task events. A fixed training log is replayed from the same initial Q-table under three conditions. FULL retains all updates, SKIP omits bad-experience updates, and NEUTRALIZE retains those updates without their event penalties. We illustrate the method on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluate it in closed-loop driving in CARLA. On the full driving task, FULL reached the goal from 33 of 40 test starts, whereas SKIP and NEUTRALIZE reached it from none, indicating that the bad experiences carry decision-relevant information. At the local level, for 47 decisions shortly before a failure of SKIP or NEUTRALIZE, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences, with a median size of one, caused the trained agent to select the failing policy's action in 46 cases. For this agent, the results indicate that its decisions can be explained by its bad experiences.

papers.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.

papers.title: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State
papers.abstract: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.

papers.title: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
papers.abstract: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.

papers.title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
papers.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

papers.title: Representing Differential Inclusions as Monads: A Framework for Compositional Controller Synthesis
papers.abstract: Sequential composition of safety-certified controllers for hybrid and non-smooth robotic systems is well studied piecewise. Yet no existing framework reduces this question to a single algebraic condition. We construct a \emph{trajectory monad} for Filippov-regular differential inclusions. Its Kleisli category treats controllers as morphisms and sequential execution as trajectory concatenation. Control Barrier Function (CBF) certification, a guarantee of forward invariance, corresponds to a sub-monad of this category. Joint safety of composed controllers then follows from one algebraic condition. All controllers must land in a common sub-monad, which is closed under the monad multiplication. The sub-monad condition recasts recasts existing CBF composition practice categorically. It explains why a smooth intersection of multiple barriers supports safe composition, while enforcing barriers phase by phase does not. For the phase-by-phase case, we derive a closed-form Bernoulli model of the failure rate. We validate it over a randomized sweep of 3{,}000 instances. The same sweep shows that the standard baseline degrades under constraint conflict as the barrier count grows. This baseline enforces all barriers simultaneously as constraints in a single quadratic program (QP). We instantiate the framework on a four-mode piecewise-affine system and on a unicycle reduced-order model over heterogeneous terrain.

papers.title: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning
papers.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at this https URL .

papers.title: AcousticBEV: Acoustic BEV Object Localization for Intelligent Vehicles
papers.abstract: Modern autonomous driving and driver assistance systems rely predominantly on cameras, radars and LiDARs for environmental perception. However, these modalities face different environmental limitations, including poor illumination for cameras and adverse weather for LiDAR. Acoustic sensing, particularly using microphone arrays, could provide complementary perception capabilities for autonomous driving, but has remained largely underexplored. In this work, we design a horizontally arranged microphone array that functions as the "ears" of a vehicle, enabling localization of nearby moving vehicles in a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation that captures both their relative direction and distance. Using this array, we collect a real-world driving dataset, AcousticScenes, which contains 2,117 static and 2,863 dynamic samples with synchronized spatial acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds and 3D bounding box annotations. Building on this dataset, we propose AcousticBEV, a learning-based method for acoustic BEV object localization, which estimates the center locations of moving traffic participants in BEV from the microphone-array signals, conditioned on the ego vehicle's own speed. Experimental results demonstrate that AcousticBEV outperforms both classical signal-processing baselines and other learning-based methods, achieving F1 scores of $47.7 \pm 1.2$% on "Easy" scenarios and $45.1 \pm 1.4$% on "Difficult" cases. Our findings demonstrate that acoustic signals from a low-cost, vehicle-mounted microphone array can localize nearby moving vehicles in both azimuth and distance.

papers.title: Distributed Shaping of Robot Swarms Through Spatial Moments of Arbitrary Order
papers.abstract: This paper shapes a swarm into a target pattern, such as a figure taken from an image, by controlling its spatial moments. The image is sampled into a reference configuration whose centroid and covariance set the position and principal spreads of the formation, while its higher-order moments, expressed in covariance-normalized (whitened) coordinates, encode the remaining shape. In contrast with geometric formation control, which prescribes distances, bearings, or relative positions between specific agents, this specification concerns the swarm as a whole and assigns no agent to a particular place. The key mechanism is orthogonalization in the swarm's own empirical inner product: projecting negative-gradient velocities onto the complement of low-degree polynomials sampled at the agents makes every higher-order correction preserve all lower-order moments exactly. The resulting hierarchical controller has lower triangular error dynamics and converges locally exponentially for any positive gains, so orders can be added without undoing those already achieved. A joint alternative regulates the higher moments together through a regularized Gauss--Newton step while preserving the centroid and covariance dynamics. We give bounds on the number of agents and sufficient conditions for regularity. Both controllers admit a distributed implementation that uses only relative positions and neighbor communication and retains local exponential convergence when estimation is sufficiently fast. In a distributed simulation on a sparse graph, 350 agents form an airplane from an unstructured swarm through moments up to order ten; the hierarchy reaches the full specification, while the joint law approaches it with smaller velocities.

papers.title: Reliable Conditioned Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability via Subsolution Learning on Exact Local Windows
papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.

papers.title: Dependable Voice Command for Multi-UAV Swarms Using Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Supervisory control of multiple autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) imposes high visual and cognitive demands on human operators, particularly when communicating mission objectives and system constraints. Voice command provides a natural interaction modality that can reduce operator workload; however, its reliability is affected by environmental noise, speech variability, and recognition errors. This paper presents a dependable voice command framework for multi-UAV swarm supervision using Small Language Models (SLMs). The proposed architecture integrates an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) module with an SLM-based semantic processing layer to transform spoken operator commands into structured task definitions for downstream multi-UAV planning and execution. To evaluate robustness, an end-to-end assessment pipeline is developed using a Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) to generate synthetic supervisory commands, which are converted into audio samples with varying operator accents and environmental signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). The resulting speech signals are processed by the ASR module, and the SLM performs contextual interpretation and phonetic correction of transcriptions when required. The evaluation isolates the resilience of the voice command pipeline under acoustic degradation and speech variation, demonstrating reliable task generation for multi-UAV supervision in challenging operational conditions.

papers.title: Frame First, Decode Once: Object-Centric Coordinates and Single-Pass Decoding for System-1 World Models
papers.abstract: Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object's initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9-2.2x for each of five decoders, and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported. Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3-29x lower latency.

papers.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at this https URL .

papers.topic_rationale: Benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in off-road environments, directly central to navigation. Contains extensive dataset-based evaluations and baseline comparisons, no real-robot deployment described.

executive_summary: Several works advance safety-critical robot control: one distills a centralized control barrier function safety filter into a multi-agent reinforcement learning policy via implicit Q-learning and synthetic near-collision states, empirically yielding collision-free navigation in 1,800 test episodes without runtime safety filters and transferring a three-agent policy zero-shot to up to twenty simulated agents and to teams of up to five Crazyflie quadrotors; another augments an inverse-Jacobian PI visual servo controller with a residual Soft Actor-Critic policy and a delay-compensated Kalman filter to reduce conveyor tracking errors from 1.1–1.4 mm to 0.3–0.7 mm on a Franka arm; a third analyzes stability failures of Koopman controllers and introduces Tangent-Invariant Koopman to match the plant’s local linearization, achieving local stabilization on four unstable benchmarks and 88% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with 0.25 ms planning; and an extension of robust safe gradient flow RL handles trajectory-level and chance constraints, with theory bounding training-time constraint violations and experiments showing zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body humanoid control and collision-free Crazyflie waypoint navigation under probabilistic safety guarantees.

New pipelines leverage limited or human-centric data for generalizable manipulation and humanoid control: AsymEEF transfers a small set of teleoperated bimanual demonstrations across heterogeneous two-, three-, and five-finger end-effector pairs via kinematic anchors, morphology-agnostic latent representations, and replay filtering, expanding replay-valid demonstrations by 16.6× in simulation and improving replay success on four simulated and six real bimanual tasks; Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation structures humanoid manipulation policy learning around tactilely observed interactions with cone-geometry multi-finger contact and online adaptation, enabling a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands to open commercial round doorknobs in zero-shot sim-to-real tests and outperforming Rapid Motor Adaptation and reactive tactile baselines; and Ego2Sim2Humanoid converts egocentric RGB-D and head-motion recordings into physically verified humanoid training trajectories through scene reconstruction, contact-band prediction, motion adaptation, and RL policy training, allowing a GR00T-based visuomotor language model to perform autonomous loco-manipulation on a Unitree G1 using only the converted data without teleoperated robot demonstrations.

Several planning and optimization frameworks target long-horizon manipulation and motion generation: Lazy-MOSAIC performs lazy skill-sequence planning using a cheap learned skill-effect world model plus selective high-fidelity simulation validation and local repair, guaranteeing fully validated skill plans while cutting expensive simulator calls and planning time on cluttered-shelf retrieval in simulation and on hardware compared with MOSAIC; RoboKit offers a GPU-based toolkit for parallel differentiable optimization with multi-seed solvers and hybrid/coarse-to-fine scene representations, running 2–60× faster than task-specific optimizers on seven tasks, optimizing 4,096 grasps in 2.97 s, and distilling optimization into policies that execute 9–240× faster at similar accuracy while accelerating RL training; and multi-CONDOR learns motion primitives with multiple discrete attractors or continuous goal contours via imitation losses that align task dynamics to latent reference systems, with Lyapunov-based convergence analysis and experiments showing ~72% RMSE reduction vs. state-machine-selected single-goal primitives and 0% out-of-tolerance starts on multi-goal benchmarks, plus successful dual-handle grasping on a Franka arm.

Navigation and control for mobile robots and autonomous driving are improved by multiple systems: a controlled ProcTHOR evaluation isolates visual factors in ObjectNav and finds surface material changes dominate performance drops while clutter and lighting matter little, with a DINOv2-based model-based agent achieving 0.83 success yet remaining appearance-sensitive; a passage-focused hierarchical multi-robot framework uses a passage-induced convex graph, soft coordination in planning, and model predictive path integral control to achieve near-perfect success and superior makespan/flowtime in 1,200 simulations and collision-free operation of eight robots; a sampling-based whole-body MPC for supported reaching on a Unitree H1-2 extends reachable workspace by ~50 cm and completes reach-and-recovery in 81% of 54 trials; a depth-aware nursing assistant platform fuses RGB-D with rule-based avoidance and NavfnROS to boost navigation success by up to 40% and clearance by 35% over single-sensor baselines; EasyNav centralizes mapping, localization, planning, and control on a shared state to cut reaction latency from 377→33 ms (indoor laser) and 71→8 ms (GPS+LiDAR) vs. Nav2 while using less compute; a Room Probability Vector-based ObjectNav policy deployed on Spot and TurtleBot reaches 0.455 success over 66 trials with an 8.4-point drop from simulation traced to sensing and layout mismatches; AgenticJevNav couples planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution for agentic search, improving simulated success to 73.33% (a 21.67-point gain over an Agent-only baseline) and achieving 70% success on a quadruped robot; and VLN-Flash provides a training-free decoder that scores short-horizon action-prefix trees in one pass, preserving the original policy’s conditionals while delivering ~3× faster decoding and up to 2.7-point gains in navigation success/SPL, along with higher success and ~160 ms lower inter-action wait time on a Unitree GO2.

Perception, mapping, and world modeling methods target efficiency and robustness: SuperGlance turns a decoder-only driving vision-language model into an encoder-style one-pass planner that scores 5,273 candidate trajectories from hidden states, supports reward-weighted and RL training, preserves VQA via multiple-choice and KL regularization, and matches or exceeds Qwen-Drive-1.0 planning performance on NAVSIM, PAI-AV, and WOD-E2E while running ~6× faster and achieving higher relative robustness when evaluation delay tracks GPU time; Polygraph incrementally fuses many drifting visual/visual-inertial odometry trajectories into a shared pose graph without a 3D map using cluster-based loop closures with learned image retrieval, metric depth, robust pose estimation, and a two-tier consensus gate, attaining comparable or better trajectory accuracy with fewer committed loop closures and faster runtime than prior work across diverse stereo, handheld, and legged datasets; Déjà-Events distills from a frozen RGB teacher into an event-only multi-view 3D model with sparsity-aware adaptive transformer gating, requiring no pose/depth ground truth and training ~1% of parameters, and achieves the lowest depth/pointmap and trajectory errors among evaluated event-based methods on EventScape and zero-shot MVSEC/DSEC, halving AbsRel on DSEC (0.15 vs. 0.30) with ~10× fewer parameters; and FlipTest introduces a three-level benchmark of visual minimal pairs, controls, and dense sweeps to test whether video world models flip predictions under small but causally critical image changes, finding 11 models perform poorly (best 18.3% pair accuracy, below 25% random) while a vision-language model and a measurement-based coding agent more accurately track the flip boundary, suggesting current pixel-prediction world models underutilize available causal state information.

Additional control and navigation contributions focus on nursing, humanoids, and language-guided driving: a supported reaching MPC for humanoids uses local sensing and environmental bracing to extend reach and maintain heavily loaded postures for over four minutes before pose drift, reaching targets in 89% of 54 hardware trials; a depth-aware navigation stack for nursing robots integrates RGB-D perception with global planning and real-time control on a Husky+Kinova platform, improving simulated cluttered-environment success and minimum clearance over single-sensor approaches and validating efficient, safety-oriented operation in real hospitals; and a safe RL framework based on robust safe gradient flows is shown compatible with PPO-style estimators, offering high-probability bounds on cumulative trajectory-level constraint violations that decay with rollouts and enabling zero-shot deployment of whole-body humanoid control and collision-free drone waypoint navigation in sim-to-real tests.

institution_matches.title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning approach that learns only from executed safe actions via implicit Q-learning and distills a centralized control barrier function (CBF) safety filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states, with theoretical guarantees that the distillation loss bounds constraint violations and per-step collision probability when distillation states cover deployed states. In simulation with multiple agents acting without any runtime safety filter and using only local observations, the distilled policies incur no collisions in 1,800 test episodes; a policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of up to twenty agents with constant per-agent computation and remains collision-free with up to eight agents. On Crazyflie quadrotors, the distilled policies are demonstrated in hardware with up to five quadrotors flying simultaneously, indicating successful transfer of the filter-free multi-agent navigation policy to real robots.

institution_matches.title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces AsymEEF, a framework that transfers a small set of teleoperated demonstrations across heterogeneous bimanual end-effector combinations (two-, three-, and five-fingered) using kinematic teacher anchors, sparse real-world X-Calib anchors, and a shared morphology-agnostic latent representation with a morphology-conditioned decoder, followed by replay filtering for executability. Across four simulated and six real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines and achieves a mean replay-valid demonstration expansion gain of 16.6× in simulation, and is further evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots.

institution_matches.title: Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes multi-CONDOR, a CONDOR-based framework that learns dynamical-system motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or continuous attracting goal contours by combining imitation learning with losses that align learned task dynamics to latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure, backed by a Lyapunov-based convergence analysis. On simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared to separately learned single-goal primitives selected by a state machine, and for tasks with two and three goals reduces the fraction of initial states ending outside goal tolerance from 0.31% and 7.29% with StableNODE to 0% in both settings. Robotic experiments with a Franka Emika arm show that motion primitives learned with multi-CONDOR can successfully grasp a container by either of its two handles, demonstrating the ability to converge to alternative valid outcomes from demonstration data.

institution_matches.title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework for long-horizon manipulation that plans over hypothesized skill outcomes using a cheap learned skill-effect world model to predict each skill’s feasibility and resulting world state, and then selectively validates only promising candidates in a high-fidelity simulator while locally repairing the search when hypotheses are invalidated. Lazy-MOSAIC guarantees that every skill in a returned plan is ultimately validated in simulation, while significantly reducing the number of expensive simulator queries compared to prior skill-centric planning approaches such as MOSAIC. On cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty, both in simulation and on a physical robot, Lazy-MOSAIC plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator calls, while matching or exceeding their success rates in all evaluated settings.

institution_matches.title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes SuperGlance, which converts a decoder-only vision-language model for autonomous driving into an encoder-style, one-pass driving policy by reading the model’s hidden state before decoding and using a linear head to score a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories, enabling supervised reward-weighted training and reinforcement learning over these pre-enumerated trajectories. SuperGlance preserves the base model’s visual question-answering ability via multiple-choice training and a KL regularization term, so that the same one-pass representation can both plan and answer visual questions about driving scenes. On NAVSIM, PAI-AV, and WOD-E2E, SuperGlance plans at least as well as Qwen-Drive-1.0 while using 84 ms of GPU time (about 6× faster), and in AlpaSim closed-loop evaluation achieves comparable km per at-fault incident up to a 300 ms delay; when delay is tied to GPU time, its advantage over Qwen-Drive-1.0 increases from 2.8× to 3.9×, although at an imposed 1.2 s delay its performance falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 operating at its own 518 ms.

institution_matches.title: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation in ProcTHOR houses where floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states are held fixed while individual visual factors (surface materials, clutter, lighting, and goal appearance) are varied, enabling isolation of how each visual change affects navigation performance. Across model-free RL, model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual encoders, the experiments show that surface material changes account for most of the average drop in success, whereas clutter and lighting changes have little effect, and even small global image statistics shifts—such as modifying only the goal object’s appearance—can significantly impair end-to-end agents. A model-based agent that plans over frozen DINOv2 image features achieves the highest success rate (0.83) under the full visual shift but still remains sensitive to surface appearance, underscoring the need for planning representations that decouple invariant spatial task structure from visual content.

institution_matches.title: Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents Polygraph, an online multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that incrementally fuses many locally accurate but drifting visual/visual-inertial odometry trajectories into a shared pose graph without building a 3D map, processing data one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time. Polygraph forms cross-session constraints by matching closed local clusters via learned image retrieval followed by sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, robust pose estimation, and a two-tier consensus gate that only admits loop-closure edges once corroborated by independent evidence, while maintaining consistency through cheap incremental solves and periodic robust batch optimizations that prune outliers. On stereo outdoor driving, indoor HoloLens and iPad traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld datasets, Polygraph runs faster than the closest prior work on the same GPU model, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and achieves comparable or better trajectory accuracy based on the prior work’s reported timings.

institution_matches.title: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Visual Servo Control with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a residual reinforcement learning approach for visual servo control in which a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller is augmented by a residual policy learned with Soft Actor-Critic in a limited-fidelity digital twin, combined with a delay-compensated Kalman filter that fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to produce latency-aware target position estimates. A frequency-domain sensitivity analysis provides a performance bound for a class of purely model-based controllers under uncertain kinematic mismatch, against which the learned residual controller is evaluated in both simulation and hardware. In experiments tracking moving objects on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda arm at conveyor speeds of 27.9–41.8 mm/s, the residual RL controller reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1–1.4 mm with the baseline inverse-Jacobian PI controller to 0.3–0.7 mm and drives errors below the derived model-based performance bound, demonstrating reliable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer despite modeling and measurement uncertainties.

institution_matches.title: RoboKit: Accelerating Parallel Differentiable Optimization for Robot Learning
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces RoboKit, a general-purpose GPU-based toolkit for parallel differentiable optimization in robotics that combines multi-seed solvers, hybrid/coarse-to-fine scene representations for geometry, rendering, and physics, and differentiable cost functions to support both optimization-based planning and learning. RoboKit’s GPU-parallel multi-seed solvers run 2–60× faster than task-specific optimization baselines across seven evaluated tasks, and its hybrid/coarse-to-fine representations enable optimizing 4,096 grasp candidates in 2.97 s by accelerating collision checking, differentiable rendering, and simulation. By distilling optimization results into policies and using its parallel simulator for reinforcement learning, RoboKit produces policies that run 9–240× faster than the original optimizers at similar accuracy, and allows RL agents to reach the performance of a GPU-based baseline up to 2.1× sooner when trained on the same simulator.

institution_matches.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
institution_matches.overview: The paper analyzes why Koopman controllers that stabilize a learned latent-space linear model may fail to stabilize the underlying nonlinear plant, and shows that nominal closed-loop stability transfers when the learned closed-loop dynamics and the true plant dynamics agree to first order on the embedding’s tangent space at the target, with a derived robustness margin for approximate matching and a proof that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly represent an unstable equilibrium. It introduces Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which uses offline transitions to estimate a local plant linearization and constrains the learned latent dynamics to match this linearization to first order while employing a bilinear predictor to capture state-dependent actuation, thereby recovering the fitted LQR gain at the target. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers learn latently stable closed loops but yield locally unstable nonlinear plants, whereas all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear systems; an offline stability test using empirical curvature successfully identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole tasks (though not under high noise), and under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, TIK achieves 88% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1–5 ms per step while guaranteeing constraint satisfaction after entering an invariant terminal set.

institution_matches.title: Déjà-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes Déjà-Events, an event-only multi-view 3D model that predicts depth, camera pose, and pointmaps in a single forward pass by distilling token representations from a frozen RGB teacher (Déjà View), requiring no depth or pose ground truth and training only about 1% of its parameters. To address event sparsity, the method introduces sparsity-aware adaptive gating that adapts shared transformer block gates to event inputs and modulates them per patch by event density so that accuracy is preserved as more refinement steps are added. Trained solely on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap and depth errors among evaluated event-based methods on EventScape and in zero-shot settings on MVSEC and DSEC, halving AbsRel error on DSEC compared with the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30) while using about one-tenth as many parameters, and also obtaining the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

institution_matches.title: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces FlipTest, a three-level benchmark (visual minimal pairs, matched controls, and dense sweeps) that probes whether video world models correctly flip their predictions when small changes in an initial frame cause qualitatively different futures. Across 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks, 11 evaluated video world models perform poorly on FlipTest, with the best model achieving only 18.3% pair accuracy—below the 25% accuracy of random guessing—and showing non-selective prediction changes that fail to track the true state boundary. On the same frames, a vision-language model and a coding agent that explicitly measures images more accurately track the flip boundary, suggesting that the necessary information is present in the visual input but current video prediction models fail to capture the causal state, motivating a rethinking of world modeling beyond pure next-frame pixel prediction.

topic_matches.title: Passage-Focused Soft Coordination for Hierarchical Multi-Robot Navigation in Bottleneck Environments
topic_matches.institution: National Research University Higher School of Economics; Peking University; Saint-Petersburg University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a passage-focused hierarchical multi-robot navigation framework that builds a passage-induced graph of convex sets and performs priority-ordered planning with two levels of soft coordination: passage-aware route selection that accounts for passage usage and traversal direction, and route-restricted continuous space-time planning that penalizes temporal conflicts. Local execution is handled by a model predictive path integral controller guided by the planned references, with adaptive temporal and geometric tracking plus selective replanning to accommodate execution deviations without rigid trajectory reservations while ensuring online collision avoidance. In 1,200 simulated instances across four environments with 5–30 robots, the framework achieves a near-perfect success rate and outperforms evaluated baselines in makespan and flowtime, and hardware experiments with eight robots complete all trials without collisions, indicating effective long-horizon coordination in bottleneck environments.

topic_matches.title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
topic_matches.institution: Amazon; Rice University; The University of Texas at Austin; University of Maryland, College Park; University of Michigan
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA), an integrated whole-body control framework for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation that structures policy learning around tactilely observed interactions, represents multi-finger contact with cone geometry, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. TMA jointly trains an upper-body manipulation policy with a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous multi-finger interaction, torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability in the round-doorknob-opening task. Trained entirely in simulation and deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands, TMA substantially outperforms Rapid Motor Adaptation and reactive tactile-policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in real-world evaluations.

topic_matches.title: Leaning Over to Reach Far-Away Objects
topic_matches.institution: University of Colorado Boulder; University of Notre Dame
topic_matches.overview: The paper studies supported reaching for humanoid robots and proposes a sampling-based whole-body model predictive control (MPC) method that explicitly leverages environmental contacts for leaning, bracing, reaching, and recovery using only local sensing and fiducial markers. Running in real time at 34 Hz on a laptop and transferring from simulation to a Unitree H1-2 humanoid, the controller extends the robot’s reachable workspace by about 50 cm beyond unbraced standing reach and can maintain heavily loaded braced postures for over four minutes before pose estimation drifts. Across 54 hardware trials spanning six targets and three table heights, the system reaches the commanded target in 89% of trials and completes the full reach-and-recovery cycle in 81%, and analysis shows that temporal persistence of sampled actions and exploration scale are key to performance, with CEM yielding the broadest robustness to planning rate and model mismatch.

topic_matches.title: Ego2Sim2Humanoid: Agentic Real-to-Sim for Learning Loco-Manipulation VLAs without Robot Demonstrations
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces Ego2Sim2Humanoid, a pipeline that converts egocentric RGB-D and head-motion recordings from glasses into physically verified robot training trajectories by reconstructing textured scenes, completing unseen surfaces when needed, and predicting target contact bands on manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, the method uses grasp planning to turn contact bands into feasible robot wrist and finger configurations, bilevel stance optimization for collision-free and reachable whole-body postures, and a motion generator plus two-stage motion correction to synthesize locomotion and out-of-view arm motions; it then trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in simulation with semantic rewards and renders synchronized robot-view data and actions. Fine-tuned solely on the converted dataset without any teleoperated robot demonstrations, a GR00T N1.7 visuomotor language action model performs autonomous loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree G1 humanoid in real-world experiments.

topic_matches.title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
topic_matches.institution: Beihang University; Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications; Harbin Institute of Technology; Nanyang Technological University; National University of Defense Technology; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder for vision-and-language navigation that scores the entire short-horizon action-prefix tree in a single forward pass using branch-specific attention and aligned token positions, exactly preserving the original policy’s conditional action distribution for each prefix. VLN-Flash computes at each depth the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative to adaptively choose how many actions to execute before re-observing, then executes the highest joint-score plan at the selected depth. On Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN, VLN-Flash yields nearly 3× faster action decoding than native autoregressive decoding and improves success rate and SPL on R2R-CE and RxR-CE by up to 2.7 percentage points, while on a Unitree GO2 it increases navigation success and reduces mean inter-action waiting time by about 160 ms after accounting for network latency.

topic_matches.title: Depth-Aware Path Planning and Collision Avoidance for Robotic Nursing Assistants Using Real-Time 3D Vision
topic_matches.institution: Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur; Indian Institute of Technology Mandi
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents a depth-aware navigation framework for robotic nursing assistants that fuses RGB-D depth sensing with rule-based obstacle avoidance and the NavfnROS global planner to handle cluttered environments with low-height and transparent obstacles that are difficult for LiDAR-only or vision-only systems. Implemented on a Husky A200 base with a Kinova Gen3 arm within a ROS-Gazebo multi-layer architecture for global planning, perception fusion, and real-time control, the system plans paths from start to goal while enforcing safety-aware navigation constraints. In simulated cluttered environments, the framework achieves up to a 40% higher navigation success rate and a 35% improvement in minimum clearance compared with single-sensor baselines, and real-world experiments further validate it as a computationally efficient and safety-oriented solution for healthcare robots.

topic_matches.title: Towards Probabilistically Safe Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Deployment on Humanoid and Aerial Robots
topic_matches.overview: The paper extends the robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to handle general trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as probabilistic collision avoidance, while allowing biased estimators of objectives and constraints and remaining compatible with algorithms like PPO. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the constraint violation during training under the proposed RSGF-RL scheme is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, decaying toward this level even from unsafe initial policies, and that the iterates converge to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Using PPO-style estimators within RSGF-RL, the authors demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone, indicating practical feasibility of the probabilistically safe RL approach.

topic_matches.title: Sim-to-Real Room-Mediated Object-Goal Navigation with ROS 2 and Nav2
topic_matches.overview: The paper deploys a Room-Mediated Co-occurrence ObjectNav policy based on Room Probability Vectors (RPVs) onto Boston Dynamics Spot and TurtleBot 4 via a robot-agnostic ROS 2 bridge, adapting sensing, localization, and action interfaces to transfer a simulation-trained semantic prior to real robots. In 66 real-world trials on Spot within a university research facility, searching for 11 object categories from two starting positions, the RPV-based policy achieves a raw Success Rate of 0.455. An analysis attributes the 8.4 percentage-point drop from the simulated Success Rate of 0.539 to factors including undetected glass walls, entry into off-limits areas, limited usable depth range, target size, and mismatches between the simulated room lexicon and the physical layout.

topic_matches.title: EasyNav: A Modular Architecture for Real-Time Navigation Across Heterogeneous Robot Environments
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes EasyNav, a ROS 2 navigation architecture that centers all mapping, localization, planning, and control modules on an explicit shared navigation state, enabling modular, representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. In real-robot indoor navigation experiments with laser sensing, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 ms to 33 ms compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, while also using less CPU and memory. In large-scale indoor–outdoor navigation experiments using GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 71 ms to 8 ms compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, again with lower CPU and memory usage.

topic_matches.title: AgenticJevNav: Agentic Object Search and Navigation via Event-Driven Verification
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces AgenticJevNav, an architecture that links goal-directed planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution for agentic object search and navigation, incorporating version, freshness, and once-only checks plus goal revision mechanisms to manage decisions and revoke obsolete actions. Across six simulated task families (60 trials), AgenticJevNav achieves a 73.33% success rate, improving aggregate success by 21.67 percentage points over a next-best Agent-only control variant under differing historical protocols. In a real-world deployment on a GENISOM L1 quadruped robot, AgenticJevNav attains a 70.0% success rate over 30 trials, including bounded search reporting, while remaining failures indicate limitations in grounding, approach planning, and runtime behavior.
